::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Part I · Clinical questions and data** · **Level:** entry · **Teaching units:** 05–08 (4 × 45 min) ·
**Required reading:** core readings of B07 and B08 (about 20 minutes) · **Lab:** [Lab W2](../exercises/lab-w2-next-word.qmd) ·
**Case sheet:** [An instruction hidden in an attachment](../exercises/casebook-w2-untrusted-instruction.qmd) ·
**No external AI account needed**
:::

## Guiding question

**Which generated statement can be checked, against what, and who checks it before it reaches a patient?**

## Learning objectives

By the end of this workshop you can

1. explain in your own words how a language model produces a fluent sentence that no source supports;
2. trace a research claim from reference and DOI to the original passage and give a reasoned verdict;
3. recognise when a real, thematically fitting source is used for a claim its study design cannot carry;
4. mark the trust boundary in a data flow where external content meets an assistant with tool access, and name one
   test that shows a blocked export stays blocked;
5. rewrite an answer for a patient so that it states uncertainty in natural frequencies, offers a choice and checks
   understanding with a teach-back question;
6. document any use of an AI tool (tool, version, date, purpose, what you checked).

## Preparation

- **Required reading** (about 20 minutes):
  [B07 · Reading an AI study critically – core reading](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b07-reading-an-ai-study.html#sec-b07-core)
  and
  [B08 · Language models in clinic and science – core reading](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b08-language-models.html#sec-b08-core).
- **Before the session:** read the two stored answers below and underline the single most contentious sentence in
  each.

## Stored answers {#stored-answers}

Both answers respond to the same *synthetic* patient question. They were written for this course to show patterns
that are typical of generated text; they are not the output of any particular system.

> **Patient question.** "I fell on my hand yesterday. The X-ray was checked by a computer program and it said
> there is no fracture. Does that mean my wrist is definitely not broken? Do I still need the follow-up
> appointment?"

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false collapse="false"}
**Stored answer A**

Good news: modern AI fracture detection is as accurate as specialist doctors. A large meta-analysis in *The Lancet
Digital Health* (Liu et al., 2019, doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(19)30123-2) showed that AI improves outcomes for
patients. A negative AI result can exclude a fracture, so the follow-up appointment is usually not necessary. If
the pain continues, painkillers and rest are enough.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false collapse="false"}
**Stored answer B**

A computer result is one piece of information, not a final answer. No test rules out a fracture with complete
certainty; some wrist fractures, for example of the scaphoid bone, may not be visible on the first X-ray. The
follow-up appointment is there to check exactly this. Tools that work well during development can perform worse
in everyday use: in an external validation, a widely used hospital model for predicting sepsis reached an area
under the ROC curve of only 0.63 (Wong et al., 2021, doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2021.2626). Please keep your
appointment and come back earlier if the pain or swelling gets worse.
:::

## Teaching units

| Unit | Task | Minutes | Observable evidence |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 05 | In R, derive next-word frequencies from twelve short sentences ([Lab W2](../exercises/lab-w2-next-word.qmd)). Use the two stored answers to examine how a plausible but false sentence arises. | 45 | Your own explanation of the generation principle and a verification task for the contentious sentence. |
| 06 | Trace a research claim from DOI and title to the original passage. In a second example the source fits the topic but the claim goes beyond its design. | 45 | An evidence card with reference, passage, verdict and documented AI use (if any). |
| 07 | A synthetic attachment contains a foreign instruction. Teams mark the trust boundary and play through, without a network, how an unintended data transfer is prevented ([case sheet](../exercises/casebook-w2-untrusted-instruction.qmd)). | 45 | A data flow with a blocked export, minimal permissions and a test that shows the blocked access. |
| 08 | Revise an answer for a patient conversation: make uncertainty understandable, name a choice and check understanding with a question. | 45 | A conversation card, plus the case card and evidence card as the first project milestone. |

### Evidence card (unit 06)

Check the two claims below. Use only the DOI resolver (`https://doi.org/` followed by the DOI), the publisher page
and the abstract or full text. If you use an AI tool at any point, record it in the last row.

| Field | Claim 1 (stored answer B) | Claim 2 (stored answer A) |
|---|---|---|
| Claim as written | "In an external validation, a widely used hospital model for predicting sepsis reached an area under the ROC curve of only 0.63." | "A large meta-analysis … showed that AI improves outcomes for patients." |
| Reference as cited | Wong et al., 2021, doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2021.2626 | Liu et al., 2019, doi:10.1016/S2589-7500(19)30123-2 |
| Does the DOI resolve to that title, journal and year? | | |
| Original passage (quote, with page or section) | | |
| Study design and what it measured | | |
| Verdict: supported / partly supported / not supported / source not found | | |
| What the answer may say instead | | |
| AI use: tool, version, date, purpose, what you checked | | |

### Conversation card (unit 08)

Rewrite one of the stored answers for the patient. The card has four lines:

1. **What we know**, in natural frequencies (for example "out of 100 people with a wrist injury like yours …"),
   labelled as an *assumption* if you do not have local figures.
2. **What we do not know yet**, in one sentence.
3. **A choice** the patient can make (for example: keep the follow-up appointment, or come back earlier if
   symptoms change), with what each option means for them.
4. **A teach-back question** that checks understanding without testing the patient, for example "So that I know I
   explained it well: what will you do if the pain gets worse before your appointment?"

## Four perspectives in this workshop

- **Ethics.** Stored answer A advises against the follow-up appointment. A wrong reassurance shifts the harm to
  the patient, who cannot check the source. The conversation card restores a choice.
- **Regulation.** If a generated text is used to inform an individual diagnostic or therapeutic decision, the
  intended purpose of the tool, not the technology, decides whether medical device rules apply; see
  [W7](w7-regulation-data-protection-incident.qmd).
- **Data protection.** Pasting a patient's question with identifying details into an external service is a
  transfer of health data to a recipient; unit 07 makes this visible.
- **Security.** Content from outside (an attachment, a web page) can contain instructions. An assistant that may
  read files and send messages must not treat such text as a command (indirect prompt injection; Greshake et al.,
  2023, [doi:10.1145/3605764.3623985](https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985)).

## Transition to W3

Your case card and evidence card form the first project milestone. In W3 the claim on your evidence card becomes a
number: what does an alert mean for the next patient, and how would you test it?

## Further reading

- [B07 · Reading an AI study critically](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b07-reading-an-ai-study.html)
  and [B08 · Language models in clinic and science](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b08-language-models.html)
  – the full chapters behind the required reading.
- [B25 · Security risks of learning and generative systems](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b25-security-risks-ai-systems.html)
  and [B23 · Data protection along the entire data flow](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b23-data-protection.html)
  – background for unit 07.
- [B21 · Ethics at the bedside and in study design](https://r-heller.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r/chapters/b21-ethics.html)
  – teach-back and shared decisions, for unit 08.
- [Scientometrics in R: Working with Full Text](https://r-heller.github.io/scientometrics-in-r/working-with-full-text.html)
  – retrieving and checking original passages at scale.
- [Scientometrics in R: Retraction Analysis](https://r-heller.github.io/scientometrics-in-r/retraction-analysis.html)
  – a source can exist and still be withdrawn.
- [Methods in R: Writing a report – Reporting guidelines](https://r-heller.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-appendices-d-writing-a-report.html#sec-appendices-d-writing-a-report-reporting-guidelines)
  – what a study must report before its claims can be checked.
- [Strategy in R: LLM Agents and Strategic Reasoning](https://r-heller.github.io/strategy-in-r/sec-llm-agents.html)
  – language models that act, not only write.
